# The Night Train

There is no better machine for thinking about time than a night train. An airplane abolishes distance; it treats the earth as an inconvenience to be vaulted. But a night train does something stranger: it lets you skip over the hours themselves. You board at eleven, surrender your shoes to the corridor, climb into a berth barely wider than a coffin, and wake up somewhere else entirely—another country, another language on the signs, another smell in the air. You have traveled four hundred kilometers without witnessing a single one of them.

I have always found this slightly miraculous. Somewhere around three in the morning, while you sleep with your face pressed against a pillow that smells faintly of other people's dreams, the train slides across a border. A customs officer may glance at your passport by flashlight, or may not bother waking you at all. Either way, you cross from one nation into another the way you cross from one dream into another: unconsciously, completely, without negotiation. In the morning you pull back the curtain and the world has been rearranged. The fields are planted differently. The church spires are Orthodox instead of Catholic. The coffee arrives in a different shape of cup.

The sleeper car is one of the last genuinely democratic spaces in Europe—or it was, once. In its narrow corridor, a professor and a plumber hang their jackets on the same hooks, brush their teeth side by side at the same tiny sink, negotiate the same unwritten etiquette of the lower bunk. There is a particular intimacy in sharing a compartment with a stranger for eight hours. You learn their snore before you learn their name. You watch them sleep, and they watch you, and somehow this is not creepy but companionable—the oldest human arrangement, strangers resting together because the road is long.

The great age of the night train was also the great age of espionage and elopement, which tells you something. The Orient Express carried diplomats and diamond thieves in equal measure. Spies loved night trains because borders were soft there, because identities could be swapped between Vienna and Budapest, because a man asleep is a man unobserved. Lovers loved them for the opposite reason: the night train was a pocket of privacy moving through the public world, a room that was nowhere, where no one could reach you. Before the telephone made everyone findable, the night train was the original airplane mode.

Of course, the romance requires some editing. The reality of night trains includes radiators that clank like a ghost demanding entry, and corridors lit all night by bulbs that no one thought to dim, and the peculiar torture of arriving at 4:40 a.m. at a station whose name you cannot pronounce, announced by a conductor who has decided that whispering is for the weak. There is the passenger who boards at midnight and eats a boiled egg in the dark. There is the moment when two trains pass each other in the night—a sound like a held breath released—and you realize that another train full of sleepers is streaming past you in the opposite direction, both of you stitching the continent together in the dark, thread against thread.

For a while it seemed the night train would die altogether. Budget airlines ate the routes; high-speed rail made even long distances fast enough to endure by day. By the 2010s, entire networks had been amputated. The night train became a nostalgia object, mourned in essays like this one, kept alive by enthusiasts the way steam engines are kept alive by men in flat caps.

And then, curiously, it came back. Climate anxiety did what nostalgia couldn't. A flight from Paris to Vienna takes two hours and dumps several hundred kilograms of carbon per passenger into the atmosphere; the night train takes fourteen and a fraction of that. Suddenly the sleeper car wasn't quaint—it was infrastructure. New routes opened. Old rolling stock was refurbished. Young people who had never known the clank of a coupling discovered that you could fall asleep in Amsterdam and eat breakfast among the Alps. The night train returned not as a relic but as an argument: that speed is not the only virtue, that the hours spent traveling are not dead weight to be minimized but part of the journey itself.

This is the deeper lesson of the night train, I think. We have built our lives around the elimination of waiting—instant messages, instant deliveries, instant answers—but some things cannot be rushed, and perhaps shouldn't be. Sleep is the most obvious one. You cannot hurry through a night; you can only be carried through it. The night train respects this. It doesn't pretend the distance doesn't exist. It simply asks you to close your eyes and let the distance happen to someone else—to the wheels, the rails, the driver awake in his cab watching the signals change green in the dark.

There is a version of this idea in almost every old story: the hero sleeps while magic carries him. Jonah in the hold of the ship. The fairy-tale princess in her hundred-year slumber, while the kingdom changes hands outside the thorn hedge. The night train is the industrial version of the enchanted boat. You give yourself over to it, and it keeps faith with you, and delivers you to the other side of the dark.

So if you ever get the chance, take the slow way. Book the berth with the scratchy blanket. Set your shoes where you can find them. Lie down and listen to the rhythm of the joints in the rail—that patient, hypnotic *da-dum, da-dum*—and let it carry you out past the edge of the city lights, out into the country where nothing is awake but the track and the moon. Somewhere ahead of you is a border, and beyond the border is dawn, and beyond the dawn is a station platform where the air smells different and someone is calling out the name of a town you've never seen in daylight.

You will arrive before you know it. That is the whole trick. That is the whole gift.
